deinde (dein)

adverb

then, next, after that

The next step in a series: prīmum … deinde … tum. Dein is the short form, which Cicero notes is often said; in classical verse the ei of both makes one syllable (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • tum — then, next; at that time

    adverb · also used · classical · Verg. G. 4.187: tum tēcta petunt, tum corpora cūrant

    Both “at that time” and “next”; in a series it often follows prīmum or deinde.

  • posteā — afterwards, later

    adverb · also used · classical · Caes. BG 1.21 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 40

    Of a later time rather than the next step.

  • inde — after that, thereupon; from then on

    adverb · also used · classical · Liv. 1.2.3 (Lewis & Short)

  • proximum est ut (+ subjunctive) — the next thing is to …, the next point is

    also used · classical · Cic. N.D. 2.73: proximum est, ut doceam deōrum prōvidentiā mundum administrārī (Lewis & Short s.v. propior); Cic. Fl. 27: proximum est ergō, ut, opus fuerit classe necne, quaerāmus (Lewis & Short)

    Moving to the next step of an argument or a task. Traupman 102 gives it for “most likely”, which it does not mean (see probably).

  • postillā — after that, afterwards

    also used · classical · Plaut. Curc. 4.2.43: numquam postillā vīdī (Lewis & Short); Traupman 42

    (vōx cōmica et poētica: Enn., Plaut., Ter., Catull.)

    Traupman writes postillāc, a form Lewis & Short does not give; the ante-classical and poetic word is postillā (or post illa). Prose says posteā.

  • proximē — next, immediately after

    also used · classical · Traupman 351

Examples

  • quid fit deinde?

    and then what happens?Plaut. Amph. 1098

  • dā mī bāsia mīlle, deinde centum, dein mīlle altera, dein secunda centum

    give me a thousand kisses, then a hundred, then another thousand, then a second hundredCatull. 5.7–9

  • Homō est prīmum īnfāns, deinde puer, tum adulēscēns, inde juvenis, posteā vir, dehinc senex, tandem silicernium.

    A person is first a baby, then a boy, then a youth, then a young man, then a man, then an old man, and at last a doddering ancient.Comen. OP 36

  • unde … dein … dein … inde …

    next comes …, then …, then …, after that …Traupman 351

See also later, some time later, a little later, probably.
